title: Dockerizing a Node.js Application
subtitle: A step-by-step guide to containerizing your Node.js apps with Docker - making deployment as cozy as a warm kitchen! 🐳

intro.title: From Chaos to Containers
paragraphs: Docker uses containers to simplify the process of creating, deploying, and running applications. With containers, a developer can pull together an application with all of its dependencies and ship it as one package.

Think of Docker containers like perfectly packed care packages - everything your application needs is bundled together in one tidy container, ready to run anywhere! In this guide, I'll walk you through creating and running a simple Docker image of a Node.js application (aka "Dockerizing"). 📦✨

items.title: Docker Installed
items.body: First, you'll need Docker on your system.

items.title: Node.js Application
items.body: A Node.js app to containerize. Don't have one? You can fork the example project.

items.title: Command Line Access
items.body: These code snippets work in bash. If you're using a different shell, you may need to adjust commands accordingly.

items.title: Create the Dockerfile
items.body: In your main application folder, create the Dockerfile. This file contains instructions to help Docker create an image of your Node.js application.

items.title: Set the Base Image
items.body: Edit the Dockerfile and add the base image. We'll use the official Node.js image as our foundation.

items.title: Create Working Directory
items.body: Add instructions for Docker to create and set the working directory for the container.

code.content:
# Create app directory
RUN mkdir -p /usr/src/app
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

items.title: Install Dependencies
items.body: The node:boron image comes with Node.js and NPM already installed. Now we install your application dependencies.

code.content:
# Install app dependencies
COPY package.json /usr/src/app/
RUN npm install

items.title: Bundle Application Source
items.body: Docker needs to bundle your application's source code inside the Docker image using the COPY instruction.

items.title: Expose Port (Optional)
items.body: By default, Docker exposes port 80. If needed, use an EXPOSE instruction for additional ports.

items.title: Define Entry Point
items.body: Finally, Docker needs instruction on what to execute when the image launches. Since our start instructions are in package.json, we'll call the start command.

blocks.title: The Complete Dockerfile
blocks.body: Putting it all together, your final Dockerfile should look like this:

code.content:
FROM node:boron

# Create app directory
RUN mkdir -p /usr/src/app
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package.json /usr/src/app/
RUN npm install

# Bundle app source
COPY . /usr/src/app

EXPOSE 8081

ENTRYPOINT [ "npm", "start" ]

callout.text: You can remove the EXPOSE line if you don't need to expose a specific port.

items.title: Package.json First
items.body: Copy package.json before copying your entire app - this way Docker can cache the npm install step and speed up subsequent builds!

items.title: Layer Optimization
items.body: Order your Dockerfile commands from least to most frequently changed. This maximizes Docker's layer caching benefits.

items.title: Port Mapping
items.body: Don't forget to map your container port to a host port when running with the -p flag so you can access your application.

items.title: Clean Builds
items.body: Use a .dockerignore file to exclude unnecessary files like node_modules and .git from your Docker context for faster builds.
